summary:
North Korea's Criminal Code of 1950, revised in 2009, appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts. Two provisions nonetheless leave enforcement to official discretion. Article 193 bans the import, keeping and distribution of "decadent culture", including sexual recordings, and Article 262 bans collective "obscene activities". Neither is defined in terms that constrain how it is applied. The US State Department's 2022 human rights report reaches the same conclusion, that no specific law criminalises same-sex conduct, and adds that the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life.

Changing the sex marker on a birth certificate or citizen card is technically possible under "unavoidable circumstances": an application to the People's Security Agency together with a state forensic medical evaluation, with surgical intervention required in practice. No law explicitly bans gender-affirming care, but the under-resourced health system makes hormones and surgery effectively inaccessible.

As of 2026 no North Korean law recognises same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Article 8 of the Family Law states that "Marriage may be done only between one man and one woman". Same-sex couples could not legally adopt children, per the US State Department's 2020 report. The Constitution, last revised 2024, does not address discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no provisions exist in law to prohibit discrimination on those grounds; the concepts do not appear.

Two dated accounts of state violence appear in the sources. A 2023 South Korean Ministry of Unification report, the 584-page "North Korean Human Rights Report", cites defector testimony alleging that at least one male detainee in a detention camp was secretly executed for homosexuality in 2014. A 2011 Korea Times report, sourced to Free North Korea Radio, claimed that a lesbian couple, a North Korean woman and a Japanese woman, were executed for being influenced by capitalism and "bringing corruption of public morals". Outright International's country page, updated 12 March 2026, records no documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people, so these allegations and that finding remain unreconciled. The most recent documented instance in the sources is from 2014; no later instance is documented.
tangentialFactors:
Official denial and official hostility run together. In April 2014 the state news agency KCNA rejected the UN Commission of Inquiry's report on the country as a political fabrication and attacked commissioner Michael Kirby as "a disgusting old lecher with a 40-odd-year-long career of homosexuality" in order to discredit it. Outright International records that KCNA denied the existence of homosexuality in 2014.

Ten years after the Commission of Inquiry report, a BBC Korean feature of 10 October 2024 documents new laws, including the Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act, that tighten control, and describes how a regime organised around the collective rather than the individual forces sexual minorities into silent self-suppression. The same feature profiles Jang Young-jin, a novelist who defected in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed, as the first publicly known gay defector; an openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017, and CNN carried his account of homosexuality's place in North Korean society and the punishment it carries in April 2017.

The US State Department's 2020 report states that there is no reliable information on LGBT persons in the country and that the regime's repression of all civil society is the dominant human-rights reality, which limits how far any external account of conditions can be verified.
localsOnly:
There is no registration route for LGBTI organisations. The US State Department states that no provisions exist in North Korean law to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or identity, and that the concepts do not appear.

Residents seeking a sex marker change must apply to the People's Security Agency and undergo state forensic medical evaluation, with surgical intervention required in practice. Gender-affirming care is not banned by law but is effectively unavailable through the under-resourced health system.

Same-sex couples could not legally adopt children as of the US State Department's 2020 report, and no relationship recognition of any kind is available as of 2026. The collective-over-individual structure of the state is documented as pushing sexual minorities into silent self-suppression.
outOfScopeNotes:
Nothing in the sources held here addresses entry or visa rules, airport or border screening, document-marker flagging, targeted inspection, bathroom or facilities access, hate-crime protection and its enforcement, or consular treatment of trans travellers. Those questions are unresolved rather than answered in the negative.

Whether Articles 193 and 262 have been applied to gender-nonconforming or trans people specifically is not sourced. No trans-specific violence figure with a denominator appears anywhere in the inventory, so no comparison against the country's general homicide rate can be made.

The two violence accounts rest on defector testimony and an external radio report; their verification status is unresolved, and they are not corroborated by the Outright International finding of no documented violence. Whether the sex-marker route has ever been used in practice, and how often, is not sourced. No survey of trans people's own experiences in the country is available; the 2020 US State Department report states that reliable information on LGBT persons does not exist.
